title: Mills, Canals and Newcomers
objective: After this level you can explain how factories, canals and Irish and German immigrants transformed the North before 1860.
summary: The Erie Canal (1825) opened the interior. Lowell’s mill girls struck in 1834 and 1836. Famine sent the Irish, and Catholic newcomers met the Know-Nothings.

cards.headline: Before the Civil War, a canal, a mill town and a famine remade the North.
cards.body: A ditch across New York, factories full of farm daughters, and ships full of Irish and German newcomers. Here is how the North changed, and who pushed back.

cards.headline: The ditch that built a city
cards.body: The Erie Canal, finished in 1825, linked the Great Lakes to New York City by way of the Hudson River at Albany. Boats could now carry people and goods between the interior and the coast. The canal opened the interior of the continent to settlement and made New York City the nation’s leading commercial center. A ditch became a highway.

cards.headline: The mill girls of Lowell
cards.body: Lowell’s textile companies recruited young women, generally 15 to 30, from New England farms that offered them few chances. The draw was monthly cash wages. The price: 12 to 14 hours a day and company boardinghouses with curfews. In 1834 and 1836 the women walked out in strikes they called turnouts, against a wage cut and then higher board charges.

cards.headline: Newcomers from Ireland
cards.body: In 1845 a blight struck Ireland’s potatoes. About one million people died in the Great Famine, and perhaps 2 million more emigrated. Most Irish who came to America settled in the cities where they landed, almost all in the Northeast. Germans came in large numbers too.

cards.headline: The Know-Nothings
cards.body: All of the Irish and many Germans were Roman Catholic, and that fed a backlash. In the 1850s the anti-immigrant, anti-Catholic Know-Nothing party flourished. The name came from its members’ instructions: asked about the movement, say you know nothing. It wanted immigrants to wait 21 years before becoming citizens.

cards.headline: Mills, canals and newcomers
learned: The Erie Canal (1825) linked the Great Lakes to New York City
Lowell’s mill girls worked long days and struck in turnouts
The Great Famine drove millions out of Ireland
Know-Nothings opposed Catholic immigrants in the 1850s

questions.prompt: What did the Erie Canal connect when it opened in 1825?

options.label: Lake Erie and the Mississippi River
options.rationale: It ran east to the Hudson and New York City.

options.label: Boston and the Lowell mills
options.rationale: Lowell is in Massachusetts, not on the canal.

options.label: The Great Lakes and New York City

questions.explanation: Via the Hudson River at Albany, it linked the Great Lakes to New York City.

questions.prompt: Why did many young New England women take jobs in the Lowell mills?

options.label: The law required farm daughters to work in factories
options.rationale: No law required it; they were recruited.

options.label: Farms offered them few chances, and the mills paid cash wages
The mills offered short, eight-hour days
options.rationale: Most worked 12 to 14 hours a day.

options.label: They were recruited from Ireland during the famine
options.rationale: Lowell recruited from New England farms.

questions.explanation: Recruited from farms that offered few chances, they came for monthly cash wages.

questions.prompt: What linked Ireland’s Great Famine to the rise of the Know-Nothing party?

options.label: The famine sent many Catholic immigrants, whom the party opposed
The party organized famine relief for Ireland
options.rationale: The party was anti-immigrant, not a relief group.

options.label: Know-Nothings blamed the famine on the Erie Canal
The famine ended immigration, so the party collapsed

questions.explanation: The famine drove millions from Ireland; Catholic newcomers met the anti-Catholic Know-Nothings.
